Anthropic just admitted that Claude Fable 5 was giving weaker responses to AI researchers without telling them.

Here's what actually happened: 

Anthropic built a hidden safeguard into Fable 5 that would invisibly degrade performance for anyone they suspected of using Claude to train competing AI models without any alert, warning message, or indication that it was happening. Researchers would just get worse results without knowing why.

Here's the timeline in 5 points:

1. Fable 5 has degraded researcher outputs.
2. Researchers got worse results unknowingly.
3. The AI community called it secret sabotage.
4. Anthropic admitted fault and reversed course.
5. Visible fallbacks now replace hidden ones.

Their view was that a hidden safeguard would be very tough to spot and work around. That argument didn't change internally until the AI research community raised serious concerns.

Dean Ball, a former White House AI adviser, called it "shockingly hostile." Prime Intellect's Will Brown was even more direct, saying it felt like Anthropic was making it harder for others to follow the same path.

The important lesson for any business using AI in production is that if your AI provider can change the system's answers without telling you and you haven't spotted it, you are not really in control of your own product.

Microsoft has reportedly restricted employee access to Anthropic's new Claude Fable 5 model over concerns linked to its data retention policy. 

Unlike other Claude models that run under Zero Data Retention, Fable 5 is part of Anthropic's Mythos-class models, which require prompts and outputs to be stored for 30 days for safety checks. 

The move has created an unusual split, as Microsoft customers can access the model through GitHub Copilot and Foundry, while Microsoft's own staff face internal restrictions until legal teams complete their review.
